doc.title: Bobby Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: School bands, Benny Goodman tunes and Marsala's chord teaching
summary: Gordon played in school groups in the late 1950s, rebelling against rock and roll with Goodman tunes, and says Marsala taught him chords and improvisation, which later helped at university.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Okay, I’ll just pick up. What was your experience in public schools as far as your clarinet playing?

Well I started before I was in high school, I started when I was around eleven or twelve years old, and then we had the usual band and orchestra you had to have in high school, and then we had little groups that would come out of that, different guys wanted to get into jazz and things like that back at that time, and so did I. And my friends I’d known through school, we’d form little groups and play for dances and little parties and things like that, and then we had the regular band and orchestra. And I didn’t take any instruction in high school, mostly through Joe Marsala, who taught me a great knowledge of chords and a great knowledge of trying to improvise on certain chord progressions. So that’s really where I got my basic start, from Joe Marsala.
When you were playing for these school dances and so forth, what year was that, what years?
Well these were 1957 and 1958, ‘56 around there.
So the popular music of that time, they were leaning towards rock & roll.

Well that’s when Elvis Presley came out, around that time. And he kind of changed everything for musicians and jazz musicians especially. Because everybody started to like rock & roll then, and that type of music. Our type of music went in the background, and it still hasn’t come back yet, but it’s starting to come through a little bit now I think.
So what kind of music would you play for school dances?
Well around that time there was a movie that came out called “The Benny Goodman Story” with Steve Allen and Donna Reed. And we used to play the Benny Goodman © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

tunes, you know, and things like that. And we played in the theatre for the original opening of the movie, in Manhasset, Long Island, just a trio — piano, drums and clarinet. And then we’d still play the old style of jazz, but we wouldn’t play any rock & roll. We were kind of against that. We were rebelling against that.
You were taking a stand. That’s interesting. Well I’m interested in how Joe taught you chords and so forth. Did he play a keyboard instrument or did he just talk about it?

No he just talked to me about it and played the clarinet and showed me certain things. I memorized a lot of the stuff that he told me and later on it came out. When I went to the University of California in San Diego and I knew exactly what they were talking about when I was studying music, because I had that instilled in me at an earlier age, about chord progressions and scales and writing and things like that. I knew how to do that way before I was in high school and way before I was in college. Because just by listening to records and listening to Louis Armstrong and listening to Eddie Condon and certain guys, Pee Wee Russell and Joe Marsala, I used to listen to records constantly, and then also got a chance, like I said, to go on the train into New York City and meet these great jazz musicians with Joe. Jack Teagarden, you name them, you can just name them just like that, off the bat, they were great. And they were always very nice to me and I looked up to them. And I always said I always wanted to be a jazz musicians like these guys. And I thought they were very successful, you know, and I said, well this is what I want to do.
